title: Canal Street shopping under segregation
summary: Tex describes black shoppers barred from trying on hats and lacking bathrooms downtown in the 1940s and 50s.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Which was more popular, the Lincoln or the Palace? Or was it?

Well, the Palace was probably the more popular. It was the larger theater, in a sense. And the, I don't know, people sort of relished going downtown New Orleans because they gave them a chance to shop at the end of the stores on Canal Street, even though at that time in history, a lot of blacks were not allowed to try on dresses and hats because I had the pleasure, or could I say pleasure, of covering a story at one of the shops on Canal Street where I went to talk with the manager. And he said he didn't want any black women trying on his hats with their greasy hair. So I wrote it in the, it was either in the former Sentinel, either Pittsburgh, Korea. I wrote the story, incidentally.
Yeah. So that was one of the problems with shopping on Canal Street for blacks?
Right, that was one of the problems because the manager thought...
What about, I'm sure, did they have separate bathrooms? Probably not.
No, well, I got news for you. Separate bathroom, if you're going to Canal Street to shop, you better go to the bathroom before you come downtown.

You know, that's a hell of a come up when you think about black men and women spending their money on Canal Street in the 40s and 50s and they didn't have bathroom facilities. You had to find your service station someplace, I hate to say a back alley, because a lot of black people were cultured and they wouldn't do that. They would probably go to the bathroom before coming home. You know.
